In [[mathematics]], the '''rational normal curve''' is a smooth, [[rational curve]] {{mvar|C}} of [[Degree of an algebraic variety|degree]] {{mvar|n}} in [[projective space|projective n-space]] {{math|'''P'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}. It is a simple example of a [[projective variety]]; formally, it is the [[Veronese variety]] when the domain is the projective line. For {{math|''n'' {{=}} 2}} it is the [[conic section|plane conic]] {{math|''Z''<sub>0</sub>''Z''<sub>2</sub> {{=}} ''Z''{{su|b=1|p=2}},}} and for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}} it is the [[twisted cubic]]. The term "normal" refers to [[projective normality]], not [[normal scheme]]s. The intersection of the rational normal curve with an [[affine space]] is called the [[moment curve]].

==Definition==
The rational normal curve may be given [[parametrically]] as the image of the map

:<math>\nu:\mathbf{P}^1\to\mathbf{P}^n</math>

which assigns to the [[homogeneous coordinates]] {{math|[''S'' : ''T'']}} the value

:<math>\nu:[S:T] \mapsto \left [S^n:S^{n-1}T:S^{n-2}T^2:\cdots:T^n \right ].</math>

In the [[affine coordinates]] of the chart {{math|''x''<sub>0</sub> ≠ 0}} the map is simply

:<math>\nu:x \mapsto \left (x, x^2, \ldots, x^n \right ).</math>

That is, the rational normal curve is the closure by a single [[point at infinity]] of the [[affine curve]]

:<math>\left (x, x^2, \ldots, x^n \right ).</math>

Equivalently, rational normal curve may be understood to be a [[projective variety]], defined as the common zero locus of the [[homogeneous polynomial]]s

:<math>F_{i,j} \left (X_0, \ldots, X_n \right ) = X_iX_j - X_{i+1}X_{j-1}</math>

where <math>[X_0: \cdots: X_n]</math> are the [[homogeneous coordinate]]s on {{math|'''P'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}. The full set of these polynomials is not needed; it is sufficient to pick {{mvar|n}} of these to specify the curve.

==Alternate parameterization==
Let <math>[a_i:b_i]</math> be {{math|''n'' + 1}} distinct points in {{math|'''P'''<sup>1</sup>}}. Then the polynomial

:<math>G(S,T) = \prod_{i=0}^n \left (a_iS -b_iT \right )</math>

is a [[homogeneous polynomial]] of degree {{math|''n'' + 1}} with distinct roots. The polynomials

:<math>H_i(S,T) = \frac{G(S,T)} {(a_iS-b_iT)}</math>

are then a [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] for the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree {{mvar|n}}. The map

:<math>[S:T] \mapsto \left [H_0(S,T) : H_1(S,T) : \cdots : H_n (S,T) \right ]</math>

or, equivalently, dividing by {{math|''G''(''S'', ''T'')}}

:<math>[S:T] \mapsto \left[\frac{1}{(a_0S-b_0T)} : \cdots : \frac{1}{(a_nS-b_nT)}\right] </math>

is a rational normal curve. That this is a rational normal curve may be understood by noting that the [[monomial]]s

:<math>S^n,S^{n-1}T,S^{n-2}T^2,\cdots,T^n,</math>

are just one possible [[base (topology)|basis]] for the space of degree {{mvar|n}} homogeneous polynomials.  In fact, any [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] will do. This is just an application of the statement that any two projective varieties are projectively equivalent if they are [[congruence relation|congruent]] modulo the [[projective linear group]] {{math|PGL<sub>''n'' + 1</sub>(''K'')}} (with {{mvar|K}} the [[field (mathematics)|field]] over which the projective space is defined).

This rational curve sends the zeros of {{mvar|G}} to each of the coordinate points of {{math|'''P'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}; that is, all but one of the {{math|''H<sub>i</sub>''}} vanish for a zero of {{mvar|G}}. Conversely, any rational normal curve passing through the {{math|''n'' + 1}} coordinate points may be written parametrically in this way.

==Properties==
The rational normal curve has an assortment of nice properties:
* Any {{math|''n'' + 1}} points on {{mvar|C}} are linearly independent, and span {{math|'''P'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}.  This property distinguishes the rational normal curve from all other curves.
* Given {{math|''n'' + 3}} points in {{math|'''P'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} in linear [[general position]] (that is, with no {{math|''n'' + 1}} lying in a [[hyperplane]]), there is a unique rational normal curve passing through them. The curve may be explicitly specified using the parametric representation, by arranging {{math|''n'' + 1}} of the points to lie on the coordinate axes, and then mapping the other two points to {{math|[''S'' : ''T''] {{=}} [0 : 1]}} and {{math|[''S'' : ''T''] {{=}} [1 : 0]}}.
* The tangent and secant lines of a rational normal curve are pairwise disjoint, except at points of the curve itself. This is a property shared by sufficiently positive embeddings of any projective variety.
* There are
::<math>\binom{n+2}{2}-2n-1</math>
:independent [[quadric (algebraic geometry)|quadrics]] that generate the [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of the curve.
* The curve is not a [[complete intersection]], for {{math|''n'' > 2}}.  That is, it cannot be defined (as a [[scheme (mathematics)|subscheme]] of projective space) by only {{math|''n'' − 1}} equations, that being the [[codimension]] of the curve in <math>\mathbf{P}^n</math>.
* The [[canonical bundle#Canonical maps|canonical mapping]] for a [[hyperelliptic curve]] has image a rational normal curve, and is 2-to-1.
* Every irreducible non-degenerate curve {{math|''C'' ⊂ '''P'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} of degree {{mvar|n}} is a rational normal curve.
